does: Cuts food into even, square-sided sticks.

intro.what: Food is cut into even square-sided sticks from a squared block.
intro.why: The shape begins before the final cut: matching slab thickness and stick width makes the pieces cook at a similar pace.

how: Peel the vegetable and trim its sides flat to make a block.
Slice the block into slabs as thick as the sticks you want.
Stack a few slabs and cut them lengthwise into sticks as wide as the slabs are thick.
Keep the trimmings for a soup or a mash.

cues.text: Sticks with flat faces and square corners, all of one thickness, so that they cook in the same time.

mistakes.mistake: Cutting from a round vegetable without squaring it first, so that the sticks come out as wedges.
mistakes.fix: Trim the sides flat before you slice.

mistakes.mistake: Slabs of uneven thickness, so that thin sticks burn while thick ones stay raw.
mistakes.fix: Hold the knife straight and take the same width at every cut.

quiz.question: Why aim for matching baton thickness?
choices: The sticks cook at a similar pace.
Uneven sticks should soften at deliberately different rates.
The shape matters but differences in thickness do not affect cooking.
quiz.because: Even thickness avoids large differences in cooking between the sticks.

quiz.question: What is done before cutting slabs?
choices: Leave the vegetable round and cut wedges.
Trim the sides to create a flat-sided block.
Slice slabs while leaving the curved outer sides in place.
quiz.because: A squared starting block gives the sticks flat faces rather than tapered sides.

quiz.question: What should batons look like?
choices: Straight sticks with flat faces and square corners.
quiz.because: The square-sided stick shape distinguishes batons from wedges or chopped pieces.

quiz.question: The sticks came out as wedges. What should change?
choices: Keep its rounded sides for the next batch.
quiz.because: Flat starting faces remove the curve that causes wedge-shaped pieces.

comes_after.why: Batons start as thick, even slices.
